title: Three and Four at Once
description: Get comfortable hitting three or four pads together for the big, full-kit accents.

steps.title: Using the whole kit
steps.description: A real drummer has two hands and two feet, and the big moments in a song often use all of them at once. On pads, that means hitting three or four at the same moment. It feels awkward at first. Try using one finger per pad and dropping them all together, or use a few fingers from each hand.

steps.title: Kick, snare and hat
steps.description: Hit the kick, snare and closed hi-hat together. All three of the core sounds in one go, which gives you a solid accent.
steps.hint: They're the first three pads on the top row, so three fingers in a line will do it.

steps.title: Kick, snare and crash
steps.description: Swap the hi-hat for the crash. This is the hit you hear when a chorus lands.
steps.hint: Kick and snare on the top left, crash (CRS) on the bottom row, second from the right.

steps.title: Kick, clap and open hat
steps.description: Kick, clap and open hi-hat. A combination you'll hear in pop and dance tracks. The open hat gives it a lift and a bit of sizzle.
steps.hint: KCK and OHH are at either end of the top row, and CLP is bottom left.

steps.title: Snare, tom and crash
steps.description: Snare, tom and crash together. Think of it as the very end of a fill crashing into the next section.
steps.hint: TOM sits right under SNR, and CRS is the next pad along from the tom.

steps.title: All four
steps.description: Kick, snare, closed hi-hat and crash, all at once. This takes some coordination, so don't worry if it takes a few tries.
steps.hint: Use three fingers on the first three top-row pads and your other hand for the crash. They only need to be close together in time.

steps.title: Starting the chorus
steps.description: The chorus is about to kick in and you want it to really land. What do you hit?
